top_choice_rationale: P002 (Rubinstein and Wolinsky) is the most mature contribution with the cleanest attribution. Rubinstein's alternating-offers model gave bargaining a non-cooperative foundation with a unique equilibrium, and the Rubinstein-Wolinsky market extension carried it into decentralised price formation. This is a branch that earlier game-theory prizes (equilibrium refinement, incomplete information, mechanism design) did not cover. Its empirical reach is indirect, and that is the main reservation. I rank P001 (Autor, Hanson and Dorn, citation limited to trade and technology exposure and local labour-market adjustment) second, ahead of P003, because of its longer record of independent replication. P003 (Chetty, Hendren and Friedman) comes third because its causal place-effect results are younger and depend on restricted data. P005 and P004 follow because credit is unsettled (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum for P005, and Helpman's split between the two) or because empirical support is mixed (P004). P000 is last because several candidates are strong enough to warrant an award.
recusal_note: No candidate-specific connection apparent from profile. None of my co-authors (Svensson, Ehlers, Erlanson, Martinello, Teytelboym, Trapp, Biró) is credited on any proposal. My market and mechanism design field is adjacent to bargaining and matching theory, which may raise my view of P002. Colleague ties through SSE affiliation with Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg are not candidate ties. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
